title: Layer 4 or layer 7: two kinds of load balancer
dek: A load balancer can work on connections or on requests. A layer 4 balancer passes each TCP connection to one server without reading it: fast, simple and ideal for long connections. A layer 7 balancer reads every HTTP request and routes by what it says: slower per request, but far more useful for web APIs. Knowing which to draw, and why, is a common interview check.

items: Layer 4: chooses a server when a TCP connection opens, from addresses and ports only, then forwards every packet of that connection there. Fast; can't see URLs, headers or cookies.

Layer 7: ends the client's connection (and TLS), reads each HTTP request, and sends it to a server over its own connections. Can route by path, header or cookie, retry, and spread individual requests.
Rule of thumb: layer 7 for HTTP APIs and websites; layer 4 for WebSockets, other long-lived connections and non-HTTP traffic, or when raw speed matters most.

body.x: A layer 4 balancer sees a new TCP connection arrive (or a UDP flow), picks a server, and from then on forwards that connection's packets to it. It doesn't decrypt or read anything. To the server, it looks almost as if the client had connected directly.

body.cap: The balancer decides once per connection. Everything inside that connection, whether one request or an hour of WebSocket messages, goes to the same server, unread.

items: Very fast and cheap: no TLS, no parsing, little memory. One balancer handles millions of connections.
A long connection stays on one server, which is exactly what WebSockets and other persistent connections need.

It can't route by URL, header or cookie, can't retry a failed request on another server, and can't spread the requests inside one connection. A client that sends everything over one HTTP/2 connection lands on one server.
TLS is handled by the servers themselves (or passed through), so they need the certificates.

body.x: Cloud examples: AWS's Network Load Balancer, Google's network load balancing, HAProxy or Envoy in TCP mode.
Layer 7: read the request, then route it

A layer 7 balancer is a reverse proxy. It accepts the client's connection, ends TLS, reads each HTTP request, chooses a server for that request, and sends it over a connection of its own (usually one it keeps open and reuses). The response comes back the same way.

body.cap: Because it reads requests, a layer 7 balancer can route by path, header or cookie, send a slice of users to a new version, and spread the requests of one client across many servers.

items: Route by content: /api to the API servers, /img to the image servers, a header or 5% of users to a canary. This overlaps with what an API gateway does.
Spread individual requests, including the many streams inside one HTTP/2 or gRPC connection.
Retry an idempotent request on another server when one fails, and add headers such as the client's real IP (X-Forwarded-For).
Stickiness by cookie when you must keep a user on one server (better to avoid needing it).

HTTP-based push, long polling and server-sent events, works well behind it: each is an ordinary HTTP request, just a slow one, so it can be routed by path like any other. Some layer 7 balancers also carry WebSockets, but a layer 4 one is usually the better home for them.
Costs: CPU for TLS and parsing on every request, a little added latency, and two connections per request path instead of one.

body.x: Cloud examples: AWS's Application Load Balancer, Google's HTTP(S) load balancing, NGINX, Envoy, HAProxy in HTTP mode.

Both kinds check their servers. A layer 4 check usually just opens a TCP connection: it proves the process is listening, not that it works. A layer 7 check requests a URL such as /health and expects a 200 within a timeout; a good health endpoint checks the server's own critical dependencies lightly, but shouldn't fail just because a shared database is slow, or every server fails together and the balancer has nowhere to send anything.

items: For an HTTP API, draw a layer 7 load balancer and mention it ends TLS and can route by path.
If the design uses WebSockets, say the connection servers sit behind a layer 4 balancer and use least connections, so each socket stays put and load stays even.
For gRPC between services, say either client-side balancing or a layer 7 balancer that understands HTTP/2, because a layer 4 one would pin each client to one server.

body.label: Go deeper: keeping a user on one server

body.x: Stickiness (session affinity) sends a user to the same server every time, by cookie at layer 7 or by hashing the client's address at layer 4. It is tempting when a server keeps something in memory, such as a half-built cart, but it fights the load balancer: a busy user's server gets busier, and when that server restarts, its users lose whatever it held.

The usual fix is to make servers stateless and keep the state in Redis or the database, so any server can answer. Affinity is still useful as a cache hint (a server is more likely to have that user's data warm) as long as nothing breaks without it.
